pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Controlling variables — hypotheses & full experimental design (KS3)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils to "ask questions and develop a line of enquiry based on observations of the real world…", to "make predictions using scientific knowledge and understanding", and to "select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, where appropriate", alongside applying "sampling techniques" and evaluating risks. This topic operationalises hypothesis-led full experimental design.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3, grades 6–8):** the 6–8 progression requires students to "plan an investigation individually and collaboratively, and in the design: identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to do the gathering, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim." The 9–12 band adds directional hypotheses specifying "what happens to a dependent variable when an independent variable is manipulated" — previewed here.

- **Operational details:** Builds directly on upper-KS2 planning with variable control (prerequisite mt_ArVBEpMAPk); parallels the general planning and structured-reasoning habits (soft links mt_QR3vxbN1o4, mt_WKxX-b86Vr). The step-up is fourfold: (1) writing a TESTABLE HYPOTHESIS in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [scientific reasoning]' — a prediction with a mechanism, not a bare guess; (2) formally naming the independent, dependent, and at least three control variables; (3) planning repeat readings and an appropriate SAMPLE SIZE for reliability; and (4) a RISK ASSESSMENT identifying hazards and control measures. Feeds forward to writing full structured reports with peer review (dependent mt_ThTbUuNb3p).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative). A learner who can write a reasoned testable hypothesis linking an IV to a DV, identify the IV, DV and at least three controls, plan repeat readings and sample size, and identify relevant hazards with control measures has met the bar. Distinguishing systematic vs random error and evaluating precision come at the next step (mt_3jmBpEepYX, mt_auJqTemMpI).
bestPractices: Teach the hypothesis as prediction-plus-mechanism: the 'because…' clause carrying scientific reasoning is what separates a hypothesis from a guess and is the assessed core — model strong vs weak 'because' clauses.

Formalise the KS2 change/measure/keep-same language into independent / dependent / control variables now, explicitly bridging from the pupils' prior vocabulary so the terms attach to an already-understood idea.
Make control-variable identification demanding — require at least three, and justify each — because at KS3 the plausible confounds multiply and 'what else could affect the result?' is the key habit.
Introduce sample size and repeat readings as reliability tools with a reason (spotting anomalies, reducing the effect of random error, enabling a mean) rather than as a ritual 'do it three times'.
Embed risk assessment as routine professional practice (hazard → who/what is at risk → control measure), normalising safety planning as part of every KS3 investigation design.
keyRepresentations: The hypothesis frame 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [reasoning]'
An IV / DV / control-variables table (with ≥3 named controls, each justified)
A full planning template: hypothesis → variables → method → repeats & sample size → risk assessment → recording
A risk-assessment grid (hazard | risk | control measure)
A predicted results sketch-graph showing the expected IV–DV relationship before data collection
commonMisconceptions: Writing a hypothesis as a bare prediction with no 'because' / mechanism, or as a non-testable statement of opinion.
Confusing independent and dependent variables, or mislabelling a control variable as the independent variable.
Treating 'repeat three times' as a rule without understanding that repeats and sample size exist to improve reliability and expose anomalies.
Naming only one or two obvious control variables and missing subtler confounds that would invalidate the result.
Seeing risk assessment as a bureaucratic add-on rather than an integral part of designing a valid, safe investigation.
Thinking a hypothesis that turns out wrong means the investigation failed — a refuted hypothesis is a valid, informative result.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–12 design a full, hypothesis-led investigation (KS3 / NGSS SEP 3): a testable hypothesis with a mechanism ('because…'), named independent/dependent/≥3 control variables, planned repeats and sample size, and a hazard-with-control-measure risk assessment. The core is coordinating this design with the epistemic distinction between validity (controlling variables so the IV's effect is what is measured) and reliability (consistency across repeats). The proposed primary approach is a design-and-run studio in which poor design is intended to produce visibly untrustworthy data; supporting approaches include variable/hypothesis classification tasks and a Socratic supervisor dialogue.

activities.title: Design studio: build it, then run it
feedback: If a control is omitted, show that the result cannot be attributed to the IV alone — name the uncontrolled variable as the confound.

If only one trial is run, show how a single freak reading drags the conclusion; as repeats increase, show the mean settle so the pattern becomes more reliable (repeats improve reliability, but only a controlled design makes it valid).
If a hazard is skipped, raise a safety flag naming the hazard and a suitable control measure.
If the 'because' clause is missing, prompt: what mechanism explains why the IV would change the DV?
If the data differs from the predicted sketch, note that a refuted prediction is still a valid, informative result, not a failed investigation.
activities.rationale: Full experimental design is a generative, multi-part construction task where each choice has consequences for validity and reliability; running the design is intended to make those abstract principles concrete and let learners feel the cost of a missing control or too-small a sample. The cited standards require planning investigations that identify IV/DV/controls, tools, recording and sufficient data.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires selecting, planning and carrying out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, using sampling techniques, and evaluating risks.

NGSS SEP 3 at grades 6-8 requires planning an investigation that identifies independent and dependent variables and controls, the tools needed, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim; 9-12 adds directional hypotheses relating DV changes to IV manipulation.
learnerActions: Write a testable hypothesis in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [scientific reasoning]', e.g. 'I predict warmer water will speed up dissolving BECAUSE particles move faster and collide more often'.
Assign the independent variable, the dependent variable, and name at least three control variables, justifying for each why it would otherwise affect the DV.
Before running, sketch the predicted IV–DV relationship as a graph showing the expected pattern.
Set the number of repeat readings and the sample size.
Complete a risk-assessment grid: hazard | who/what is at risk | control measure.
Run the planned (simulated) investigation and inspect the data it returns, comparing it with your predicted-results sketch.
Deliberately leave one control out (e.g. don't fix water volume), re-run, and compare how interpretable the results are.
Run a single trial versus many repeats and watch how an anomaly affects the mean.
activities.intendedInsight: Validity and reliability are properties you build into a plan: an uncontrolled variable makes results muddied and unattributable (a validity problem), while too few repeats let one anomaly swing the mean (a reliability problem). More repeats do NOT rescue a confounded design.

activities.title: Sort, judge and match (variable and hypothesis practice)
feedback: For a mislabelled variable, re-check: 'is this the one thing I deliberately change (IV), the thing I measure (DV), or something else that would otherwise affect the DV?' — if it is something else that could affect the DV, it should be controlled.
For a bare prediction such as 'more concentration = faster' chosen as a hypothesis, point to the absent 'because' / mechanism.
For a mismatched hazard, show the specific control measure that reduces that risk.
activities.rationale: Classifying variables, judging whether a hypothesis is testable and reasoned, selecting adequate sample size, and matching hazards to controls exercise the curriculum-required skill of identifying IV/DV/control variables against clear criteria. This builds and checks the component skills, though on its own it does not let the learner feel reliability consequences in live data.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires selecting, planning and carrying out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, using sampling techniques, and evaluating risks.
learnerActions: For an acid-concentration-affects-reaction-rate scenario (e.g. hydrochloric acid reacting with marble chips), sort the quantities (concentration, rate/time, temperature, volume, surface area, same apparatus) into independent / dependent / control.

From several hypotheses — including the bare prediction 'more concentration = faster' and the reasoned 'increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions' — choose which are both testable AND carry scientific reasoning, and say what is wrong with the rest.
Match named hazards to appropriate control measures.
Set repeats/sample size for the scenario and justify the choice (spotting anomalies, enabling a mean, reducing the effect of random error).
activities.intendedInsight: Variable roles, hypothesis quality, hazard control and sample-size adequacy can each be judged against clear criteria; a hypothesis needs a mechanism, and a control is something that would otherwise affect the DV.

activities.title: Supervisor challenge dialogue
feedback: Push on any vague mechanism until the reasoning is explanatory, not merely directional.
When a confound is overlooked, ask what else varies that could change the DV.
Separate validity from reliability explicitly if the learner swaps or merges them.
activities.rationale: A supervising-scientist persona can pressure-test hypothesis reasoning and control identification Socratically. It is a proposed supplement, best used after the studio, since dialogue alone cannot execute the design to demonstrate validity and reliability in data.
learnerActions: Present a hypothesis and plan to a lab-supervisor persona.
Respond to Socratic challenges: 'Is that testable?', 'What else could affect your DV?', 'Is three repeats enough — and what does that fix?', 'Are your results valid, reliable, or both?'.
Revise the 'because' clause and the control-variable list in response to the questioning.
activities.intendedInsight: Pressure-testing the reasoning behind a hypothesis and hunting for subtler confounds can strengthen the 'because' clause and surface missed controls.

constraints: The assessed core is the 'because…' mechanism clause: a hypothesis must be a reasoned, testable prediction, not a bare directional guess or a statement of opinion.
Require at least three genuine control variables, each justified as something that would otherwise affect the DV; naming only one or two obvious controls misses subtler confounds.
Treat repeats and sample size as reliability tools with a reason (spotting anomalies, reducing the effect of random error, enabling a mean), not a ritual 'do it three times'.

Keep validity and reliability distinct: controls → validity (the right thing is measured); repeats → reliability (consistent readings); accuracy → closeness to the true value. More repeats do not make a confounded design valid.
Embed risk assessment as routine design practice (hazard → who/what is at risk → control measure), not a bureaucratic add-on.
A refuted hypothesis is a valid, informative result; a hypothesis turning out wrong does not mean the investigation failed.

The classification/matching tasks and reference plans build or check components but do not themselves let learners experience reliability consequences in live data; the dialogue cannot run the experiment. A labelled reference of a completed plan is a reference, not the main teaching activity.
Formalise the KS2 change/measure/keep-same language into independent/dependent/control variables, bridging explicitly from prior vocabulary.
Distinguishing systematic vs random error and evaluating precision belong to a later step, not this one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted a 'static image cannot support' this skill and that design reasoning 'is not spatial'. These are presented as narrowly scoped affordance observations (a fixed reference plan cannot be reconfigured and run), not as universal laws; a labelled reference plan can still support learning as a reference.

The 'poor fit' claims for image-only and 3D formats were catalog comparisons; retained only as the limitation that those formats do not support constructing and running a plan, without asserting comparative efficacy.
The UK DfE source is marked verified:false in the row; the standards claim is retained as cited but not independently confirmed here.
The relative strength of the studio over the classification and dialogue formats is a design proposal, not a tested-efficacy finding.

Self-audit: the worked example particle-collision mechanisms (warmer water → faster particle motion → faster dissolving; higher concentration → more particles per volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate) are scientifically consistent and retained as illustrative hypotheses, not as the only acceptable answers.

probeDeeper: Why does your hypothesis include a 'because'? What would be missing without it?
You take three close repeats but left temperature uncontrolled — are your results reliable? Are they valid? Can they be one without the other?
If a classmate got very consistent results from a test that changed two variables at once, would you trust their conclusion? Why or why not?
How does your number of repeats or sample size affect how much you trust the pattern?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong plan states a reasoned hypothesis ('increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions'), correctly assigns the independent variable (concentration) and dependent variable (rate/time), names at least three genuine controls (temperature, volume, same apparatus, surface area…), plans repeats (e.g. three runs, take a mean) and an adequate sample, and identifies hazards with control measures. Crucially it distinguishes VALIDITY (controlling variables so the test actually measures the effect of the IV) from RELIABILITY (consistency across repeats), and treats the hypothesis as a testable prediction with a mechanism, not a guess.

errorPatterns.pattern: Validity/reliability conflation: thinks taking more repeats makes a confounded test valid, or calls a well-controlled test 'reliable' as if the words were interchangeable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate them explicitly: controls → validity (the right thing is measured); repeats → reliability (consistent readings); accuracy → closeness to the true value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The valid-vs-reliable explanation swaps or merges the two ideas.

errorPatterns.pattern: Hypothesis as bare prediction: 'more concentration = faster' with no mechanism or 'because'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the 'because…' with a particle-collision mechanism so the hypothesis is explanatory, not just directional.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The stated hypothesis predicts an outcome but gives no scientific reasoning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weak or mislabelled variables: lists fewer than three genuine controls, or names the dependent variable as something to control.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Three-column IV/DV/control sort; check each control is something that would otherwise affect the DV.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The variable list is short, or assigns the wrong role to a variable.

responseLevels.gap: Gives a bare prediction with no mechanism, lists too few or muddled variables, or treats 'more repeats' as what makes a test valid.
responseLevels.full: Produces a complete, reasoned plan (mechanistic hypothesis, correct IV/DV, at least three justified controls, repeats and sample size, hazards with controls) and cleanly distinguishes validity (control → right thing measured) from reliability (repeats → consistency) and accuracy — coordinating design and epistemic reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Writes a reasoned hypothesis and identifies IV/DV/controls and repeats, but conflates validity with reliability, or can't fully justify the sample size and controls.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're planning an experiment on whether the concentration of a sugar solution affects how fast a reaction happens. Talk me through your full plan: your hypothesis and the reasoning behind it, which variable you change, which you measure, at least three you must control, and how many readings or repeats you'd take and why. Then explain the difference between making your results VALID and making them RELIABLE.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The valid-vs-reliable distinction is the discriminator: a student can list controls and repeats yet conflate the two — thinking more repeats fix a confounded design, or calling a well-controlled test 'reliable'. A strong response ties controls to validity and repeats to reliability, and gives the hypothesis a mechanism rather than a bare prediction.
